subject: Badly shaped histogram of posterior p-value

messages.author: a96aa45411c16ae6
messages.subject: Badly shaped histogram of posterior p-value
parts:
Hello,

Now I am fitting a model which predicts PM2.5 concentration with other pollutants such as PM10, NO2, and SO2.
All pollutants were previously log-transformed. My formula is as below:
formula.lot <- logPM25 ~ 
  f(FID, model='bym', graph=filepath, scale.model=T) +
  f(TMSID.f, logPM10, model='iid', hyper=list(prec=list(prior='loggamma', param=c(0.3,0.0001)))) +
  f(TMSID.f2, logNO2, model='iid', hyper=list(prec=list(prior='gaussian', param=c(0,0.7)))) +
  f(TMSID.f3, logSO2, model='iid', hyper=list(prec=list(prior='gaussian', param=c(0,5))))

Remarks: The variables FID and TMSID.fx are identifiers of monitoring stations.

Here are my results. First, PIT histogram seems almost flat if zeros are ignored.


Second, thanks to Blangiardo and Cameletti(2015:168), I have investigated posterior predictive p-value with code as below:
predictive.p.value <- c()
for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
predicted.p.value[i] <- inla.pmarginal(q=data[,field][i], marginal=inla.fit$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])
}

Unfortunately, shape of the histogram of posterior predictive p-value looks too weird.


Even though previous threads said that there might be a model mis-specification or a systematic error, I can't figure out what was a problem. 
There was no problem when I checked the model-fitting procedure thoroughly(with verbose=TRUE).

Can I get some help?

Thanks in advance.

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Badly shaped histogram of posterior p-value
parts:
its more likely a modeling/data issue than a computational one. I just
notice your rather unstandard proors for the log-precisions, like this
prior transferred to the stdev scale,

hist(sqrt(1/exp(rnorm(10000, mean=0, sd = 1/sqrt(5)))), n=100)

is very informative

H
